newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's markets still confident on re-election.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's markets still confident on re-election.

text.p: Delays and setbacks failed to scuttle market confidence that a constitutional amendment to let Brazil's President Fernando Henrique Cardoso run for a second term will be approved, analysts said.
"The market still believes the bill will pass. What's less clear is the timing of the approval," said Deiwes Rubira de Assis, a senior vice president at ING Barings in Brazil.
Investors and analysts see re-election as essential for the success of the government's economic reform efforts and many had expected the Chamber of Deputies to approve the amendment this month.
But the largest party in Congress poured cold water on government and market hopes for quick passage of the bill when it voted Sunday at a convention to oppose the measure.
The Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB), a government ally, surprised Cardoso by recommending that its members in Congress delay until February 15 a vote on the measure and then reject it.
A lower house committee had been set to vote on the amendment today, but deputies postponed the vote until Wednesday, allowing the government more time to consolidate its support among PMDB members.
Analysts now believe the chamber will not get around to voting on the amendment until late February, with final congressional approval likely to come in late March or early April.
Rubira de Assis recognized the market was overly bullish on re-election and now will take a more realistic view of what it will take the government to secure the bill's passage.

"Approval of the re-election amendment will require more political negotiating, take longer and cost government coffers more," he said. The behaviour of Brazilian bolsas Tuesday was evidence that investors' feet are back on the ground regarding re-election.

After falling Monday on concerns over re-election, local stocks rebounded early Tuesday as investors overcame the initial emotional reaction and rebuilt positions, despite uncertainties over the re-election agenda.
Analysts also said the delay in the voting process should not be a surprise for investors familiar with the slow pace of decision making and deal cutting involved in Brazilian politics.

"This is part of the game," said one banker, who asked not to be named. "Nobody could expect the re-election's approval to be so easy. Any major congressional decision always has to involve compensations, bargaining."
Others were confident a re-election amendment would pass, even if the government is forced to hold a referendum on the issue in the event Congress rejects the bill.
"Re-election will pass, either through Congress or via a plebiscite," said Rene Aduan, financial director of private bank Banco Real.
Although it has been the driving issue behind local stock trade, some analysts say the market is exaggerating the importance of re-election.
"Many think Brazil will sink into chaos if re-election is not approved. That's not true," said Paulo Ferraz, president of private bank Bozano, Simonsen.
Re-election would be positive, but the Brazilian economy is on the right track with or without it, he added.
